chapter_theme: Two songs at Kurattai (குறட்டி): the poet asks not to sink in the mud of women's bodies with a mind bound to maya, and not to wander in a ruined body of diseases, filth and carrion; the praise names Siva the beggar of alms and a long litany of Parvati.
structure_note: 893 is a courtesan song; 894 catalogues the body's diseases.

893.reading: The poet lists the sharp eye-corners, mountain breasts, red lips, belly, speech, bangled hands and loosened girdles of the price-women, and asks whether he will wander with a mind joined to maya, sinking daily in their mud and wasting his days. The praise names Vishnu of the Garuda banner who destroyed Ravana's army, as uncle, and Murugan the son of the Lord who flayed the elephant and took alms while women's girdles and bangles slipped in shame, at Kurattai with its walls and balconies.
893.nuance: சேறு தனில் நித்தம் மூழ்கி நாள் அவம் இறைத்து: the women are mud and the days are poured away. மாதர் மேகலை வளைக்கை நாண மாபலி முதற்கொள் நாதன் appears to name Siva as the beggar (Bhikshatana) whose beauty made the sages' wives lose their girdles and bangles.

894.reading: The poet lists the diseases, diabetes, leprosy, phlegm, wind, bile, piles, fever, and the worms of the house Brahma built of blood, brain, flesh, skin and pus, stinking through nine gates, a puppet of disease that foxes, dogs, ghouls, vultures and owls will eat, and asks whether he will wander in vain carrying this ruined body. The praise is a litany of Parvati as Narani, the woman of dharma, lady of the six faiths, Mahamayi, the dancer, the blue one, queen of the Vedas, Uma, Neeli, bearer of the trident, full of jnana, who gave birth to the hero on the peacock, at Kurattai of mansions, towers and groves.
894.nuance: நான்முகன் எடுத்த வீடு: the body is a house Brahma built, and the inventory runs from disease through its stuff to its scavengers. The praise is given almost wholly to the Mother (ஆறு சமயத்தி, ஞானபூரணி).

links.note: Both name the scavengers that will eat the body, foxes, dogs, ghouls and vultures, with owls in 894 and flies, ants and crows in 898; 894 uses them to end its catalogue of disease, 898 to shame those who still swagger in palanquins.

893 asks whether he will wander, sinking daily in the mud (சேறுதனில் நித்தம் மூழ்கி) of the price-women and pouring away his days. Kural 919 calls the soft shoulders of women who draw no line the mire (அளறு) in which base men sink (ஆழும்). The song takes the Kural's image of the mire, and adds the daily repetition and the wasted days.

894 calls the body a house Brahma built of blood, brain, flesh, skin and pus that stinks through nine gates (நவத்துவாரம் நாறும்), a puppet of disease to be eaten by foxes and dogs. Naladiyar 47 calls it a pot oozing filth from nine openings (ஒன்பது வாய்ப்புலனும்), which the fool addresses with love's epithets because of its dark skin. Both make the nine openings the proof of the body's foulness; the Naladiyar aims at desire, while 894 aims at the wish to carry the body in vain.
